ANIMAL CATEGORIES LESSON · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Insects — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the six-legged crew and their big jobs, one insect at a time.

What is this?

Insects are animals with six legs and a body in three parts — head, middle and tail-end. There are more insect kinds on Earth than all other animals added together.

What does it mean?

Small does not mean unimportant: insects pollinate our food, recycle the garden and are lunch for birds and frogs — the world runs on small workers.

What does the child need to know?

All insects have six legs (count them!); the bee drinks nectar and makes honey; the ladybug — called ladybird in Britain — eats aphids that hurt plants; the dragonfly hunts other bugs mid-air.

Why this matters

Insects are a child’s first wild animals — findable in every garden, park and windowsill, no zoo required.

What it teaches

Counting to six on real creatures, careful observation without touching, and gentle-catch-and-release ethics: look, learn, let go.

Words to learn

insectsix legsbutterflybeehoneyladybugladybirddragonflywingsantennae

Say this to your child

“"Insects have six legs and big jobs! The bee makes honey and carries pollen, the ladybug — ladybird, in Britain — guards the garden, the butterfly used to be a caterpillar, and the dragonfly flies like a tiny helicopter. Six legs, look and count!"”

Step by step

  1. The rule first: we look with our eyes, never our hands — bugs are wild friends, not toys.
  2. The butterfly: it hatched from a caterpillar that ate and grew, built a chrysalis, and came out with wings. A whole second life!
  3. The bee: it sips nectar and carries pollen between flowers — that is how fruit starts. Honey is its winter pantry.
  4. The ladybug: garden police — it eats hundreds of aphids. In Britain the same beetle is the ladybird; both names, one bug.
  5. The dragonfly: four wings that work separately — it can hover, fly backwards, and it eats mosquitoes. The pond’s helicopter.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the butterfly sits wings-open, the bee hovers beside a flower, the ladybug shows its red shell with black spots, and the dragonfly stretches its four long wings in an X.

Ask your child

"How many legs does every insect have?" (six) "Which insect makes honey?" (the bee) "What did the butterfly used to be?" (a caterpillar)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count six legs on every bug they meet for a week, patrol the garden announcing "ladybug police!", or refuse to squish a spider "because the ladybug said so".

Out in the real world

Spring and summer in the US, UK and Canada are insect seasons — a ten-minute garden hunt finds all four card insects most weeks. Beekeepers visit schools; honey straight from the comb is the tastiest show-and-tell.

Try it together

Bug-hunt bingo: draw a 2×2 card of your own with butterfly, bee, ladybug and dragonfly, and walk the block until every square is spotted. Eyes only, whisper voices, big checkmarks.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many legs does an insect have?" (six) "What does the ladybug eat?" (the bugs that hurt plants) "How does the butterfly begin?" (as a caterpillar)

This lesson pairs with the Insects flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animal Categories.
